summary: Gives guidance on using DKIM with mailing list managers, based on deployment experience. Lists often change messages, which can break signatures, so this best current practice explains how to handle such scenarios.

eli5.summary: A mailing list is like someone who reads your letter aloud to a group. This explains how DKIM signatures can still make sense when the list adds its own notes to the message.

subtitle: Best practices for keeping DKIM useful when mailing lists rewrite the messages that pass through them.

tldr.problem: Mailing list managers often change messages before reposting them, which breaks the sender's DKIM signature and can trigger wrong filtering or policy actions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives advice to authors, mailing list managers and receivers: the list should verify the incoming signature, record the result, remove broken signatures and add its own signature to the message it sends.
tldr.outcome: Lists that sign their own output take responsibility for what they send, and receivers can judge the list's signature instead of a broken author signature.

today: RFC 6377 is a Best Current Practice, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 6376 (DKIM Signatures) and RFC 5617 (ADSP).

sections.title: Why Lists and DKIM Clash
sections.content:
DKIM lets an administrative domain take some responsibility for a message by adding a cryptographic signature. Ordinary relays make no substantive change to a message, so the signature stays valid. Mailing List Managers (MLMs) are different: they take delivery of a message, reformat it and repost it, often invalidating the signature.

The RFC explores four questions: when an author should sign mail sent to lists, what an MLM gains by verifying DKIM, what removing existing signatures costs, and what adding its own signature means. It says these are open questions with no definitive answers, and that the suggestions are largely predictive, without substantial implementation history behind them.

Its best general recommendation is that the MLM, or an MTA in its domain, applies its own DKIM signature to every message it forwards, and that receivers take the MLM's domain signature into account.
sections.eli5: Lists copy and change letters, so the original seal breaks. This memo explains what everyone should do about it.

sections.title: Roles and Types of Lists
sections.content:
The RFC names roles: the Author, the Originator (often the Mail Submission Agent), the Signer, the Verifier and the Receiver. It also defines a message as "DKIM-friendly" if an intermediary makes no change that makes a valid signature fail.

There are four kinds of MLM:

  • Aliasing: changes only the SMTP envelope recipients and adds trace header fields. Its output continues the author's original transit.
  • Resending: may change the message, and its output counts as a new message.
  • Authoring: creates the content itself, such as newsletters and bulk marketing.
  • Digesting: a special case of resending that bundles recent submissions into one message.

The RFC focuses on resending lists, because they conflict most directly with DKIM. It splits their work into MLM Input, where the list is the receiver, and MLM Output, where the list is the author and signer of a new message.
sections.eli5: Some lists just pass letters along untouched. Others copy them, change them, write their own, or bundle many into one.

sections.title: How Lists Break Signatures
sections.content:
A signature fails to verify if any part covered by its hashes changes. The RFC lists what resending MLMs commonly do:

  • Subject tags: adding a list name such as [example] to the Subject breaks signatures that cover that field.
  • List header fields: adding fields for list functions is not a concern, since DKIM tolerates added header fields.
  • Other header fields: adding or replacing Reply-To or Sender can break signatures that covered them.
  • Minor body changes: footers or headers change the body hash. Limiting the body length covered by the hash would avoid this, but it has security implications.
  • Major body changes: reformatting MIME parts or flattening HTML to plain text will invalidate a signature.
  • MIME part removal: replacing large parts with URLs breaks the signature unless a body length limit was used.

Even if a list passes messages unmodified today, a configuration change or software upgrade may change that.
sections.eli5: Adding a sticker to the outside or a page inside your letter changes it, so the seal no longer matches.

sections.title: Lists That Do Not Know DKIM
sections.content:
A non-participating MLM treats DKIM and Authentication-Results header fields as having no special meaning. An author sending signed mail to such a list risks recipients seeing a message that appears to be from the author but carries a signature that fails. Some mail filters wrongly penalize such messages, even though DKIM says an invalid signature is to be treated as no signature.

If a domain publishes a strict policy under ADSP (Author Domain Signing Practices), the originating site SHOULD use a separate message stream, such as a subdomain, for personal mail that may go through lists. Sites wanting a "discardable" ADSP setting SHOULD keep that tightly controlled stream apart from mail that transits lists.

Receivers cannot reliably tell that a message came through a non-participating list. Sites whose users subscribe to such lists SHOULD not apply strict DKIM-related handling to those users' mail. Where a "discardable" policy applies, participants SHOULD honor it. One option is to "wrap" a non-participating MLM between DKIM-aware components.
sections.eli5: If the helper does not understand seals, your sealed letter may arrive looking tampered with. It is safest to use a different seal for club letters.

sections.title: What Participating Lists Should Do
sections.content:
Mere additions of header fields are the most DKIM-friendly change. Body headers and footers are common and not expected to fade. The l= body length tag could bound the signed part but is not workable for MIME messages and has security considerations, so its use is discouraged. The RFC recommends using standard header fields rather than body text to express list parameters.

A resending MLM SHOULD reject outright any mail from an author whose domain posts a "discardable" ADSP policy. At subscription, an ADSP-aware MLM SHOULD check the subscriber's domain and either refuse the subscription or warn. The RFC gives an example where a receiver rejects a list message, the list sees bounces and removes that subscriber.

A suggested sequence for the list:

  1. Attempt verification of all DKIM signatures on the input.
  2. Apply local policy to authenticate the author.
  3. Optionally remove existing Authentication-Results fields.
  4. Add an Authentication-Results field with the results.
  5. Remove the previously evaluated DKIM signatures.
  6. Add a new signature covering the whole output message, including that new field.

DKIM-aware resending and authoring MLMs SHOULD sign their own output. Selective signing is NOT RECOMMENDED, because it creates a signed and an unsigned stream. A list message that cannot be authenticated MAY be held for moderation or rejected.
sections.eli5: A good helper checks your seal, writes down what it found, takes off the broken seal and puts on its own, so everyone knows who sent the copies.

sections.title: Receivers, Feedback Loops and Reporting
sections.content:
Receivers SHOULD treat a signed list message like any other signed message. A receiver that trusts a particular list may extend that trust to an Authentication-Results field signed by it, and SHOULD ignore or remove such fields that are unsigned or not from a trusted domain.

For rejections at SMTP time, the RFC says code 550 is the correct response, and a 5.7.0 enhanced status code SHOULD be used so lists can tell policy rejections from other delivery failures. For a "discardable" ADSP policy, the receiver SHOULD instead accept the message at the SMTP level and drop it without delivery.

On Feedback Loops (FBLs), MLM operators SHOULD register with FBLs from major providers and share which signing domain the list uses. Because authors cannot control a list, an FBL report sent back to the author is not actionable. MLMs SHOULD also apply DKIM failure-reporting mechanisms when they are available.
sections.eli5: When a message is turned away on purpose, the helper should be told it was a rule and not a typo, so it does not remove a member by mistake.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC introduces no new technology. It points readers to the Security Considerations in the DKIM, ADSP and Authentication-Results specifications.

It adds one warning about relaying Authentication-Results. Receivers generally should not trust such data without a good reason, such as a prior agreement with the list's domain. Such agreements are strongly advised to require that those header fields be covered by a DKIM signature added by the list's domain.
sections.eli5: Only trust a note that says "I checked the seal" if you trust whoever wrote it and it carries its own seal.
